definition.text: A heterodox, non-equilibrium school of economics that grew out of Keynes's General Theory and was developed by Kalecki, Robinson, Kaldor, Weintraub and others.

facts.text: Its foundation is the principle of effective demand: demand matters in the long run as well as the short run, so a market economy has no automatic tendency toward full employment.
Unlike new Keynesians, post-Keynesians do not blame market failure to deliver full employment on sticky prices or wages.
They stress that money supply responds to bank credit demand, so a central bank can only manage the interest rate; mainstream policy now largely targets the interest rate.

Strands include Kalecki's class-based effective demand, Kaldor's increasing returns, Davidson's focus on time and uncertainty, Minsky's financial fragility, stock-flow consistent models and Modern Monetary Theory.
Cambridge Econometrics built the post-Keynesian-based E3ME energy-environment-economy model, which the European Commission uses to analyse the effects of its environmental and economic policies.

definition.text: A model for describing and analysing the flows of materials and energy through cities, as in a city-level material flow analysis.

facts.text: Abel Wolman developed the term in 1965, modelling the inflows and outflows of a hypothetical American city of 1 million people, mainly water and the waste it produces.
Herbert Girardet contrasted circular metabolism, where nearly everything is reused, with the linear metabolism of cities, with clear resource inputs and waste outputs.
Howard T. Odum's energy method coined emergy, measuring the solar energy used directly or indirectly to make a product, in solar equivalent joules (sej).
Material flow analysis became the mainstream school because its units are more practical for the public, officials and researchers.
Four uses for planners are sustainability reporting, urban greenhouse gas accounting, mathematical modelling for policy analysis and urban design.
